Renew Holdings plc (RNWH-GB): a high-quality, predictable compounder whose 18-month return is too thin to buy today

Written 22 October 2026 by the Investment Analyst for Richard. Share price 959p on 16 October 2026. The basis of the figures, the sources and the definitions of "consensus" and "the model" are in the end-notes.

Share price, 16 Oct 2026959pmarket value about £760m

Fair multiple11.0–11.6xguideline 10.79x; sell-side 12.3–13x

VerdictNot a buy todaybuy on a deferral sell-off to 9.8–10.5x, or on confirmation by the November and May prints

Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The decision: do not buy Renew today; buy it at either of two defined entry points. Renew is a high-quality, low-risk business, but its shares offer only a dividend-plus-earnings return, the next two results are skewed to the downside, and no re-rating mechanism is in sight. The 18-month expected return is roughly nil to plus 3 percent.

Entry point 1: on weakness
A sell-off to 9.8 to 10.5 times earnings after clients defer work. Renew's operating leverage, record order book and net cash make that sell-off a buyable event, as April to October 2025 showed.
Entry point 2: on confirmation
The 24 November 2026 and May 2027 results confirm organic growth at about 5 percent, and the new chair announces a reset of the financial framework. The multiple can then revisit 12.5 to 13 times.

The three dated tests that decide between these paths are set out in #9.

What Renew is. Renew Holdings is a United Kingdom engineering-services group that maintains and renews safety-critical infrastructure for regulated or state-owned clients: rail track and structures, water networks, electricity distribution lines, strategic roads, the Sellafield nuclear site and onshore wind turbines. Renew works under about 250 long-term frameworks with its own accredited crews, and it is the only listed pure play in United Kingdom utility and rail maintenance.

Renew's financial profile is that of a quality business. Revenue is £1.19bn. The adjusted operating margin has held between 6.4 and 6.7 percent for five years. Return on capital employed is 22 percent (27 percent on the five-year average). The balance sheet holds net cash before leases, and the dividend is progressive.

The investment case in one paragraph. Renew sells into five legislated, five-year spending cycles that all run to 2029-2031, and three of those cycles (water, the electricity grid and roads) ramp up at the same time through FY29. Renew's own revenue troughed in FY25, when organic growth was minus 2.5 percent on the slow start of Network Rail's Control Period 7, and has since turned. Organic growth was about 5 percent in FY26 (2.2 percent in the first half, about 7 percent in the second); the order book is a record £945m at March 2026, conservatively defined as firm twelve-month task orders; profit is a record; and the balance sheet holds net cash after four bolt-on acquisitions in twelve months. The model has adjusted earnings per share compounding at 6 to 9 percent a year, from about 70p to 71p in FY26 to about 88p to 89p in FY29, on a flat margin of 6.5 to 6.6 percent. That growth needs no leverage, no price increases and no cost programme. It does include £30m to £40m a year of acquisitions at 7 to 8 times EBITDA, which consensus does not model. The shares trade at 11.6 times 24-month-forward earnings, exactly their ten-year median.

The five conclusions that matter for the decision.

1
Predictability
Renew is a predictable compounder, not an inflection story. The direction and three-year level of Renew's earnings are about as secure as any contractor's: I put a 75 to 80 percent probability on FY29 adjusted earnings per share landing between 80p and 95p. But the growth rate has been reset from about 10 percent a year to 6 to 8 percent. The margin cannot expand from either side, because Renew has no real pricing power, no cost lever, and contracts that hand its efficiency gains to clients. The supply of accredited labour, not demand, caps organic growth near 5 percent. Nothing in the next 18 months changes the growth rate.
2
The risk
The main risk is the timing of client work within a half-year, and over the next 18 months that risk is skewed to the downside. One variable, when regulated clients call off work, moves earnings by 10 to 12 percent in the half-year in which it lands; in January 2025 it caused a 9 percent forecast cut and a 22 percent one-day share-price fall. Most of the dated events to spring 2027 are risk events: the 28 October Budget (rail and roads are taxpayer-funded, and a £428m cut to Road Investment Strategy 3 is already proposed); the formation of Great British Railways in 2027 (procurement friction on 40 percent of revenue); the first-half FY27 comparison against a record winter of reactive rail work; and water clients' finances (Thames Water needs £2.4bn to keep operating to autumn 2027). I carry a client-deferral branch at 20 to 25 percent probability, with FY27 earnings per share of 64p to 68p and the shares at 600p to 680p.
3
Expectations
Guidance gives no cushion, and trading alone will not move consensus. The company guides "in line" with its house broker's forecast; the three brokers sit within 2 percent of each other; revisions are flat; all three rate the shares a Buy. The only source of upgrades that does not depend on a client is the steady addition of acquisitions, which is reliable but small (1 to 2 percent of earnings per share a year). The one event that could add a further leg is a reset of the financial framework or a capital return under the new chair, Pete Raby (in post from 27 January 2027), which I put at 35 to 40 percent probability during 2027.
4
Cash
Renew's cash record is weaker than the narrative claims, and cash is the least verified line in the model. Of the last three "cash beats", two were one-offs (lower cash tax in FY25; a £6.9m insurance receipt in FY26) and only one was genuine. Underlying pre-lease net cash at September 2026 was £6.3m: flat on FY25 and about £6m below the model. The house broker models a £30m working-capital outflow over FY26 and FY27, against £2m to £3.5m a year in the model, so I have moved the model's working-capital input toward the broker's (a cash-only change; see the end-notes). The balance sheet published on 24 November will settle the question.
5
The return
The return is modest, and it comes from earnings rather than from the multiple. At Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for a Bottoming stock (10.79 times), the model's total shareholder return is plus 3.5 percent to September 2027 and plus 11.1 percent to March 2029, because a 7 percent de-rating eats most of the earnings growth. In my view, 10.79 times prices the deferral branch as if it were the base case. My fair multiple of 11.0 to 11.6 times gives plus 6 to plus 11 percent over 18 months and plus 14 to plus 19 percent over three years. Weighting the branches by probability brings the 18-month expected return back to roughly nil to plus 3 percent, because the deferral branch's price effect (minus 20 to 25 percent) is larger than the upside branch's (plus 20 percent).

1Tailwinds in the operating environment; absence of headwinds

The tailwind is that Renew's clients must maintain their assets; the headwind is that the clients choose when. Regulators and statute oblige Renew's clients to maintain their networks and set the budgets five years at a time. The same clients decide when, within each five-year period, the work is called off, and several of them are under financial or political strain.

Five funded spending cycles underpin demand, and all five run to 2029-2031.

CyclePeriodSizeWhat matters for Renew
Rail: Network Rail Control Period 7Apr 2024 to Mar 2029£45.4bn£19.3bn of renewals, flat in real terms after about £1.3bn to £2bn of inflation erosion; renewals running at 83% of plan (Office of Rail and Road, July 2026)
Water: Asset Management Period 8Apr 2025 to Mar 2030£104bn70 to 100% above the previous period and back-end loaded into 2027-2029; £3.4bn of reopener money provisionally approved in August 2026; Pennon alone lifted its plan by £1bn to £3.6bn in October 2026
Power: Ofgem's electricity distribution and transmission controlsdistribution to Mar 2028; transmission from Apr 2026£22.2bn; £28bn to £31bntransmission investment above £90bn by 2031
Roads: Road Investment Strategy 3Apr 2026 to Mar 2031£27bnrenewals up about 75%; the £14.5bn second Scheme Delivery Framework starts April 2027
Nuclear: Sellafield decommissioninguntil 2125about £4bn a yeara long-dated, steady budget

Two further shifts help Renew. Government policy has moved explicitly toward low-cost care of existing assets rather than new enhancement, which is Renew's end of the market. And competition has thinned: 3,805 construction insolvencies in the year to June 2026 removed capacity, so the surviving contractors bid for margin rather than volume.

Demand is structural and visible, but it reaches Renew's revenue with a lag and a cap. Client budgets would allow double-digit growth in water, grid and roads. The supply of accredited labour, however, caps what any contractor can deliver at mid-single-digit growth: the sector needs 50,000 extra workers a year, and 90,000 rail workers leave the industry by 2030. The external environment therefore supports three things: organic growth of about 5 percent (water 10 percent, power 15 percent, highways 7 to 9 percent, rail nil, nuclear and wind recovering); a margin that the environment neither expands nor compresses; and a range of outcomes whose downside is deferred work rather than lost work.

Four headwinds, three of them dated, are real but manageable.

The Budget
28 October 2026
The Budget faces a deficit of nearly £12bn and 30-year gilt yields at 6 percent. Taxpayer-funded clients (rail, roads and nuclear, roughly 60 to 65 percent of revenue) are exposed; ratepayer-funded clients (water and grid) are not.
Great British Railways
2027, then April 2029
The new body unifies track and train by 2027. It brings administrative friction now and centralised, benchmarked procurement at the Control Period 8 re-let from April 2029.
Water regulation
Reopeners now; price review 2029
The Water White Paper abolishes Ofwat in favour of a new super-regulator, and political backlash on water bills adds uncertainty to reopeners and to the 2029 price review.
Water-company balance sheets
Slow-moving
Pennon's £550m rights issue, South East Water's downgrade and Thames Water's £2.4bn emergency funding show the strain. Every water client underspent its year-one allowance (Yorkshire Water's variance was £142m, 90 percent of it timing).

Regulators' penalty regimes keep these headwinds manageable, because the regimes make maintenance the last spending a stressed client cuts. FY25 proved the point: Network Rail deferred renewals and redirected the money to reactive work, and Renew's operating profit still rose.

Where I differ from the market. The narrative (Deutsche Bank and the company) presents the five spending cycles as the whole story. Nobody covering Renew connects it to the water analysts' evidence of year-one client slippage, or to the rail regulator's finding that renewals run at 83 percent of plan. I therefore expect the water ramp to arrive more in FY28 than in FY27, and I treat "rail flat" as an assumption that depends on reactive volumes staying near their weather-driven record.

What would change my view. Upward: a Budget that protects rail and roads capital in real terms; reopener determinations in December 2026 that confirm the back-end load in water; Pennon's and United Utilities' plan uplifts reaching Renew's task orders in FY27. Downward: a real-terms cut to Network Rail's Control Period 7 or to Road Investment Strategy 3; Thames Water entering special administration with a payment freeze.

Score: 62.Legislated, non-discretionary demand to 2030 is a rarer tailwind than most European companies have, but the client-side financial and political strain has risen over six months and the transmission into Renew is capped at mid-single-digit growth.

2Internally-driven corporate change forces; absence of problems

Renew's strategy is complete and resourced; the one live force for change is the new chair. The internal change forces protect the predictability of earnings more than they change the growth rate.

The strategy is set, not changing. Renew is a pure-play, asset-light maintenance group funded by its clients' operating budgets, with a stated financial framework: organic growth above 5 percent, a margin of 6 to 7 percent, free cash conversion above 60 percent, return on capital employed of about 27 percent, and net debt below 1 times EBITDA.

The three concrete strategic moves of the last two years are complete:

  • The building exit. Walter Lilly was sold in October 2024 at nominal value with its liabilities transferred, a move worth about 40 basis points of group margin.
  • The power transmission and distribution platform. Excalon (June 2024), Emerald Power (October 2025, at 4.1 times EBITDA), PWR-X and EDES (May 2026) have been assembled into a turnkey design, underground, overhead and jointing offer at 11kV to 132kV.
  • The water footprint for Asset Management Period 8. Renew has grown from 3 water-company clients in the previous period to 10 of the 12, with 29 framework positions and sole-partner status on two Welsh Water lots.

Joint bidding across Renew's brands wins work that no single brand could. The ARQ, AGE, AGC and SBE joint ventures have won £626m of frameworks in three years, and four brands are bidding together for the second Scheme Delivery Framework.

Governance has been tightened, though one step is late. Long-term incentives now split between relative total shareholder return, earnings per share growth and free cash flow growth, and the executive shareholding requirement has doubled to 200 percent of salary. An external internal-audit provider is being appointed in 2026, which is late for a ten-brand acquirer carrying £135m of unbilled contract assets.

The one live change force is the chair. Pete Raby joined as chair designate on 5 October 2026 and succeeds David Brown at the annual general meeting on 27 January 2027. Raby ran Morgan Advanced Materials for a decade. The board has chosen an industrial operator with a record on margins and capital allocation to succeed a chair from transport operations. Renew is now a ten-brand acquirer with an untouched balance sheet and a target framework that it has not raised in years, and Raby's record (below) contains exactly what that framework lacks. His most likely first act is a capital markets day in 2027, which Deutsche Bank flagged on 1 October 2026 and to which I give a 35 to 40 percent probability. None of his possible first acts is announced.

The problems are real but small.

  • Full Circle (onshore wind) is the one piece of evidence against management's acquisition judgement. Bought in October 2024 for £49m to £51m at about 10 times EBITDA, Full Circle is Renew's only move outside the United Kingdom regulated regime. It lost a major client to insolvency and is restructuring a French unit whose underperformance the company calls "severe". The drag is £2m to £3m of operating profit.
  • Civil nuclear is depressed by site-wide industrial action at Sellafield, with no stated end date.
  • The executive team is stretched. The executive board is two people, and the chief financial officer is also company secretary and the investor-relations contact. The two are running four integrations, a French restructuring and a board transition at once.
  • Pay optics are poor. Executive salaries rose by up to 42 percent over two years, at the moment of the first profit warning in twenty years, which matters for the pay vote at the January annual general meeting.
  • Employee engagement has slipped: the employee survey response rate fell from 78 to 70 percent.

So what: the internal forces deliver steady acquired growth, and only the chair could lift the growth rate. The internal forces deliver 3 to 5 percent a year of acquired earnings growth at 4 to 10 times EBITDA, a progressive dividend and a margin held within its target range. The chair is the one force that could lift the growth rate, and that is a 2027 event with a 2028 earnings effect.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side expects Raby to keep the focus on acquisitions; his record says he also returns cash when deals are scarce. I weight a change in capital allocation higher than the narrative does, and a margin programme lower, because Renew's margin is set by its contract forms, not by management (#5).

What would change my view. Upward: a capital markets day with a dated framework; a return-of-capital policy; the Full Circle restructuring reported complete. Downward: a larger power platform deal at 10 times EBITDA or above, while private-equity consolidators (M Group Services, Network Plus) bid up the same assets.

Score: 55.A coherent, well-executed programme that is now largely in the base, with one credible new agent of change (the chair) and ordinary acquirer friction.

3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

A supportive industry structure and a real but narrow moat give Renew high, durable returns without pricing power. Those returns last as long as Renew retains its frameworks and its crews, and nothing else protects them.

The industry structure is favourable, with one fragility: the client sets both the price and the timing. Procurement weights 70 to 90 percent on quality, safety and reliability and only 10 to 30 percent on price, so a competitor cannot buy market share with price, and an incumbent cannot charge for quality.

ForceAssessment
Barriers to entryHigh. Accreditation (rail, nuclear, high-voltage); the cost of bidding (up to £2m per rail framework); incumbency (seven-year frameworks, with Renew retaining 95% against an 80% sector average); and, above all, owning accredited crews in a market that loses them faster than it trains them.
Competitor conductRational, and enforced by the clients' rules. The tier-one contractors (Balfour Beatty, Kier, Morgan Sindall, Costain, Galliford Try) have spent a decade de-risking after Carillion's collapse and now run target-cost and cost-plus books; the regional contractors lack the balance sheet for a price war.
SubstitutesWeak and slow. Clients cannot bring the work in-house, and predictive monitoring reduces reactive work only over a decade (and Renew supplies that monitoring).
SuppliersBenign.
ClientsThe fragility. Clients set the price and the timing of work, and the clients are themselves under strain.

Renew's moat is scarcity and incumbency, and it confers no pricing power. The scarcity is accredited labour: Renew directly employs its crews (an audited average of 4,583 workers in FY25), self-delivers about 60 percent of its rail work, trains 368 to 400 apprentices and retains more than 90 percent of its workers. The incumbency is about 250 frameworks, reached nationally through ten regional brands that can combine in joint ventures, and fed by a decentralised acquisition model that keeps founders in place and that competitors cite as distinctive. The moat widens without management action as labour grows scarcer and as the water footprint matures. Clients, however, capture Renew's efficiency gains: the ARQ joint venture saves one client up to £10m on a £50m electrification scheme. That transfer of efficiency to clients is why framework retention is high and the margin is flat.

Renew's financial profile is stronger than any United Kingdom contractor's. Renew's EBITDA margin of 8 percent is about twice the United Kingdom contractors' and below only Keller's (chart below), and its EBIT margin of 6 to 7 percent compares with 2 to 4 percent at the three United Kingdom contractors. Capital spending is 0.6 percent of revenue, free cash flow is 0.9 times net income, and net debt including leases is 0.2 times EBITDA. Return on capital employed of 22 to 27 percent is two to three times the cost of capital; it drifts toward 19 to 20 percent only because acquired goodwill accumulates.

The financial profile has four weaknesses:

  1. No pricing power.
  2. A persistent gap of 20 to 25 percent between adjusted and reported earnings, from acquired-intangible amortisation (£9.2m, rising to £12m), employment-linked deferred consideration treated as remuneration, and Allenbuild legacy claims in discontinued operations.
  3. Working capital that has drifted from minus 7.5 percent of revenue in FY21 to minus 1 percent at March 2026, as water and acquired businesses dilute rail's favourable payment terms.
  4. Unbilled contract assets of £135m under cost-to-cost revenue recognition, which the auditor names as its key audit matter.

Management is excellent at what clients reward and ordinary at what investors reward. Paul Scott (chief executive since October 2016, 24 years at Renew, shares worth 471 percent of salary, no open-market sales) and Sean Wyndham-Quin (chief financial officer since 2017, shares worth 333 percent of salary) are a long-tenured, heavily invested team with operating backgrounds. They run a deliberately low-ambition, high-consistency model. Their record: revenue up 80 percent and earnings per share up 63 percent in the five years to FY25; one profit warning in twenty years (disclosed early, then beaten); no equity issued since 2010; candid disclosure of bad news; and a conservative order-book definition.

The two executives excel at delivery, safety and framework wins, which clients reward. They are ordinary at margin expansion, capital returns and acceleration, which investors reward: the framework targets have not been raised despite being exceeded for years, and the chief financial officer re-anchors every results call to the middle of the target range. The culture matches the economics: Renew takes no fixed-price lump-sum work, and safety comes first on every board agenda.

So what: the structure is unusually supportive for a contractor, but less so than an oligopoly. Procurement rules protect the supplier's margin and statute protects the client's budget. The structure still gives Renew no pricing power and leaves all timing risk with the client.

Where I differ from the market. Deutsche Bank's argument for a "20 percent discount to United Kingdom business-services compounders" treats Renew's moat as deserving a compounder's multiple. I think the moat is real but is a scarcity-and-incumbency moat without pricing power. Until the margin shows it can move, such a moat earns a contractor-plus multiple (11 to 13 times), not a business-services multiple (15 times or more).

What would change my view. Downward: the loss or material re-cut of a Network Rail framework, or a rail safety event. Upward: evidence that the power platform wins design-and-build lots at the electricity distribution re-let from April 2028, against Balfour Beatty's stated pivot into distribution.

Score: 64.A high-return, net-cash, asset-light model in a supportive structure with proven management, held back by the absence of pricing power and by client concentration (Network Rail about 40 percent of revenue).

4Conservative guidance; track record of delivery and upgrades

Renew gives no numeric annual guidance, so the house broker's forecast serves as guidance, and it leaves no cushion. Four times a year the company says whether trading is "in line with the board's expectations", and the market reads that statement against the house broker's published forecast. The medium-term framework (#2) is the only numeric guidance, and it has never been raised.

The framework is conservative against history and roughly fair against the next three years. Over the last five years organic growth averaged 9 percent, cash conversion averaged 69 percent, and the margin never left its target range. The 9 percent uses the company's own definition, which counts post-acquisition growth as organic from day one; the statutory definition gave minus 2.5 percent for FY25. Once rail's flat real budget and the labour cap are allowed for, the inputs support organic growth of 5 to 6 percent over the next three years, close to the framework.

Management's informal commentary runs modestly ahead of the numbers. Management promised a "significant" second-half acceleration and delivered it, and describes water as "tracking ahead" and the pipeline as "extremely active".

Correction: the claim that Renew "consistently beats on cash" must be withdrawn. Of the last three year-end and half-year cash beats, FY25's £10m beat came from lower cash tax and FY26's from a £6.9m insurance receipt on historical claims. Underlying pre-lease net cash at September 2026 was £6.3m, exactly in line with consensus and flat on FY25. Cash conversion is still good (63 percent in FY24 and FY25, and 71 percent in the first half of FY26, on the company's measure). The accurate description of Renew's cash record is "meets, with one-off help", not "beats".

So what: the guidance convention gives consensus credibility but no cushion. A positive surprise shows up as a 1 to 3 percent broker nudge; a negative surprise shows up as a 9 to 12 percent cut. Renew's conservatism sits in the medium-term framework, where it cannot be "beaten" on a results day. The realistic upgrade path from trading over 18 months is therefore small, and the first explicit raise of the framework, if it comes, is a 2027 event under the new chair.

Where I differ from the market. Consensus and the narrative treat Renew's cash record as a strength and do not interpret the insurance receipt. I treat cash as the least verified line in the model until the 24 November results.

What would change my view. The 24 November results setting FY27 expectations above the house broker's current £82m of operating profit (I put that at 25 percent probability), or the company adopting numeric annual guidance.

Score: 55.Conservative in framework, fair in annual number, no cushion; a clean delivery record on profit with one external miss and a cash record that is sound but not the serial beat the narrative claims.

5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out scope, feedback loops

Renew passes inflation through but has no real pricing power, its operating leverage works only in reverse, and its one unused lever is the balance sheet. Revenue growth converts into profit growth one for one at best.

Pricing power: nominal pass-through, no real price. Renew's contracts are target-cost, cost-reimbursable or indexed schedules of rates, with task durations of days to months, so wage and materials inflation flows into rates within one or two reporting periods. The proof is the margin record: the gross margin stayed between 13.2 and 14.4 percent and the operating margin between 6.4 and 6.7 percent through cumulative input inflation above 20 percent, the April 2025 rise in employer National Insurance and a 6.2 percent rise in the National Living Wage. Price contributes about 3 points a year to revenue and nothing to margin.

There is no instance on file of a Renew rate card rising faster than cost inflation, and there are three structural reasons why none will:

  1. Price is scored in procurement.
  2. Clients run contractual efficiency mandates: Network Rail's £3.9bn Control Period 7 efficiency target, Ofwat's price control deliverables and, to come, Great British Railways' benchmarking.
  3. Retention pay absorbs the value of labour scarcity.

Real price can move only at re-procurements. A small gain is possible at the second Scheme Delivery Framework (April 2027) and at the electricity distribution re-let (April 2028); the Control Period 8 re-let (April 2029) is a risk.

Operating leverage: a half-year timing exposure with negative asymmetry. Renew's directly employed crews are paid whether or not work arrives, while most other costs are called off task by task.

Volume that arrives as planned drops through to profit at roughly the gross margin, 13 to 14 percent. Volume withdrawn at short notice costs 20 to 25 percent, because the accredited crews are paid regardless and are not cut: crews made redundant during a deferral cannot be rehired for the catch-up. The seasonal pattern provides a free calibration: first-half margins run at 5.6 to 5.7 percent and second-half margins at 7.3 to 7.4 percent on the same cost base, so a swing of roughly 10 percent in productive volume moves the margin about 170 basis points. The first half of FY25 showed the effect in practice: revenue rose about 14 percent and adjusted operating profit fell 3 percent on deferred rail task orders. Over any period longer than a half-year there is no positive operating leverage, because productivity gains are shared with clients.

At Renew, operating leverage and client call-off timing risk are the same thing, and this memo treats them as one variable.

Financial leverage: unused, and a store of optionality. Pre-lease net cash was £13.2m at September 2026 (£6.3m underlying), and lease liabilities are about £32m. Renew has a £140m facility to October 2029 at a margin of 150 basis points, a self-imposed ceiling of 1 times net debt to EBITDA (about £100m) and a covenant of 2 times. Net financial items fall from £4.6m in FY25 to about £2.7m in FY26 and £1.5m by FY30. The chain below shows what a buyback would be worth and how likely one is.

The probability rises toward FY29 because the surplus cash builds under a chair whose record includes buybacks.

Cost-out: none available, and none needed. The identifiable items are the French restructuring (£1.5m to £3m), the end of the FY26 overlap in deal costs (£1m) and the end of the Sellafield dispute (£2m to £4m, which is a volume recovery rather than a cost saving), offset by about £1m of added central cost. The decentralised model has no shared-service layer to harvest, and cutting crews would cut the next framework win. Peer precedents (Balfour Beatty's 40 percent cut in operating expenses, Kier's £115m of savings) repaired broken, centralised groups and do not apply to Renew.

Feedback loops: two reinforcing loops add growth, and three balancing loops hold the margin flat. The strongest reinforcing loop, with the best evidence in the file, runs from the water footprint through collaboration to contract retention: 8 of 10 water regions are at or ahead of plan. The second reinforcing loop, still early, runs from specialist acquisitions through self-delivery to larger turnkey lots in power; the AGE joint venture is already winning rail electrification lots. Of the three balancing loops, the loop from acquisition multiples to goodwill is mild, but it marks the "false friend" path: organic growth falling below 3 percent while acquisitions continue. The net effect of all five loops is about one point a year of organic growth above a contractor that merely holds its market share, a flat margin, and perhaps 5 basis points a year of margin from mix.

So what: revenue growth does not produce outsized profit growth at Renew. Profit grows in line with revenue, and the asymmetry is to the downside in any half-year in which a client defers work. The one lever that could make earnings per share grow faster than profit is the unused balance sheet, and that lever is in nobody's base case.

Where I differ from the market. The pricing report's headline of "robust pricing power" rests entirely on pass-through; I side with the evidence that real pricing power is absent, not latent. Earlier Viewforth work carried the deferral scenario's margin at 6.0 percent, which is the mild end of the range. On the company's own calibration, organic growth 2.5 to 4.5 points below plan on today's larger fixed cost base takes the margin to 5.5 to 6.0 percent.

What would change my view. A full-year margin above 7 percent would be evidence of mix (power, marine and wind at their target margins), not of self-help; a margin below 6 percent would be evidence of deferral, not of cost inflation. A buyback announcement would change the per-share arithmetic by 6 percent for every £50m returned.

Score: 40.Reliable inflation pass-through and a comfortable balance sheet, but no real pricing power, no cost lever, no positive operating leverage and an untapped financial lever; revenue growth converts to profit growth one for one at best.

6Forecast financials; scope for double-digit growth; scope for higher growth or margins than the past

The base case is earnings per share growth of 6 to 9 percent a year on a flat margin; double-digit growth needs the balance sheet or a chair-led reset. The model runs ahead of consensus from FY28 only because consensus models no further acquisitions.

Below the operating line, the effects roughly net out. The tax rate normalises from 21.6 to 25.5 percent in FY26, a one-off 5 percent cost to earnings per share growth that consensus already includes. Lower net finance costs add 2.5 percent. The share count is flat, and the dividend grows about 5 percent a year at a 30 percent payout.

Double-digit growth is not in the base case and is possible only with the balance sheet. Earnings per share growth of 6 to 9 percent a year is the shape of the base case. Double-digit growth would need two of the three levers below. None of the three is in the model, and all three are plausible under the new chair from 2028.

Against the past, the forecast shows lower growth, the same margin and better cash. Revenue grew about 12 percent a year over FY20 to FY25 on FactSet's basis, helped by a 25 percent year, a 19 percent year and larger deals; the forecast is 6 to 7 percent. The margin has been 6.4 to 6.7 percent for five years and is forecast at 6.5 to 6.6 percent. The one line forecast above history is cash: free cash flow of £55m to £74m a year, against £25m to £43m historically on FactSet's narrower measure. The reasons are structural (no working capital tied up in building work, and smaller deals), but the working-capital question in #4 and #9 qualifies the cash forecast.

The model matches consensus for FY26 and FY27 and runs ahead from FY28, because consensus models no further acquisitions. The model is in line with consensus on FY26 and within 1.4 percent on FY27. Its 75.3p cross-check for FY27 is 1.7 percent below consensus, reflecting a 25.5 percent tax rate, a slightly higher finance cost, and half of the Sellafield and French recovery deferred to FY28. The model is 1 percent above consensus in FY28 and 5 percent above in FY29. Consensus shareholders' equity rises to £407m by FY29, which shows that the brokers assume the cash is retained rather than spent on acquisitions; for the same reason, the model's revenue is above consensus in every year. The model's equity free cash flow (£54.7m in FY26) is above FactSet's consensus free cash flow (£48.0m) because the model uses a wider definition.

Where I differ from the market. I am slightly below consensus on FY27 and above it on FY28 and FY29. The difference from history rests on two drivers, "water up, rail flat"; both are decided by client timing, and neither is visible in Renew's disclosures until it is printed. The segment sizes behind the forecast path are less well established than the path itself: water is 13 or 22 percent of revenue depending on the definition, power £55m or £80m, and wind £22m or £30m. That uncertainty changes where the growth must come from, not how much growth there is.

What would change my view. Downward: a second-half FY26 organic growth rate below 7 percent, or a first-half FY27 rate below 2 percent. Upward: a water organic growth rate printed above 12 percent, or a capital markets day that sets a margin target range of 6.5 to 7.5 percent.

Score: 45.Predictable mid-to-high single-digit earnings growth on a flat margin is above the European median for visibility and below it for slope; there is no scope for growth or margins above the past without the balance sheet or a chair-led reset.

7Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over 6-12 months

Upgrades over the next 6 to 12 months will come from acquisitions and a possible 2027 reset, not from trading. The results most likely to bring a cut fall in spring 2027; the positive events cluster beyond 18 months.

The timeline below carries my probabilities for each result; three points need explanation. At the 24 November results, FY27 expectations are most likely held at the house broker's £82m of operating profit and 76.6p of earnings per share; an upgrade of 1 to 2 percent would come from annualised acquisitions and water momentum, and a trim of 1 to 3 percent from tax, finance costs and the French restructuring. At the January annual general meeting, Raby's first words are more likely to promise a review than to change a number.

Spring 2027 is where a cut is most likely. The April trading update and the May interims (in line 65 to 70 percent, a 5 to 12 percent cut 20 to 25 percent, an upgrade 10 percent) carry four pressures at once: the first-half comparison against the record reactive winter in rail; the first half under Budget-adjusted rail and roads budgets; the friction of Great British Railways' formation; and the water clients' year-two phasing. Late 2027 is where the skew turns positive. The FY28 expectation set at the FY27 results will include the second Scheme Delivery Framework at full run-rate and the electricity distribution outcome, and is more likely to be set above today's consensus than below it.

Three reasons why consensus will not move on trading:

  1. The "in line" convention removes the beat.
  2. The house broker's model already contains the water ramp. Water supplies 40 percent of the incremental earnings in Deutsche Bank's driver model (chart below), so a water beat has to be large to show.
  3. The one independent model with a visible figure already sits above the house broker. Peel Hunt forecasts 77.0p and 83.5p, so an organic growth print at the house broker's own estimate of 7 percent for the second half changes nothing.

What does move the consensus number is acquisitions. Brokers add each bolt-on on the day it is announced: Deutsche Bank added 1 percent to FY27 and FY28 for Edwards Diving and PWR-X on 12 May 2026. At £30m to £40m of deals a year, acquisitions provide a reliable upgrade of 1 to 2 percent a year, and the build-up of equity in consensus forecasts proves that consensus excludes it. Beyond acquisitions, a capital markets day with a raised framework would lift FY28 and FY29 earnings by 3 to 6 percent through the margin, and a buyback would add about 6 percent to earnings per share for every £50m returned (#5).

So what: the probability-weighted path for consensus is roughly flat for FY27 and upward for FY28. For FY28, I put a 45 percent probability on consensus being raised by 2 to 5 percent, 35 percent on it being held and 20 percent on a cut. With only three contributing brokers, net breadth of revisions is a near-binary statistic: it reads nil until an event moves all three brokers the same way, and a deferral would do exactly that.

Where I differ from the market. The narrative holds our base case with no cushion, and it under-weights the only branch that would move the number by more than 3 percent, which is negative. The market also does not price the two positive drivers beyond 18 months: the acquisition drip and the reset.

What would change my view. Evidence on 24 November that second-half FY26 organic growth was 8 percent or more with a 7.4 percent second-half margin, which would start an upgrade story; or the announcement of a capital markets day.

Score: 42.A small, reliable positive revision drip from acquisitions and a possible 2027 reset, against a convention that makes a trading-driven upgrade cycle unlikely and a 20 to 25 percent chance of a cut in spring 2027.

9Riskiness and simplicity of forecasts and expectations

The case is simple to trace in arithmetic, but its one key variable is undisclosed, lands inside half-years and is amplified by an illiquid share register. A 10 percent earnings miss would be a 25 to 35 percent share-price event.

Simplicity is high. Renew has one segment, one country (99 percent of revenue), one contract philosophy (no fixed-price lump sums), one margin range and one key variable. The chain from regulated budget to earnings per share is simple arithmetic (below), which is why the three brokers sit within 2 percent of each other. The operations beneath the arithmetic (which task orders, from which client, in which half-year) are not disclosed, so the case can be traced in arithmetic but not in operations.

Five key judgements drive the value of the shares over one to two years. The sensitivities below use the model's FY27 base: revenue of £1,270m, adjusted operating profit of £82.7m, adjusted earnings per share of about 75p to 76p, 79.3m shares and a 25.5 percent tax rate.

  1. Water converts at about 10 percent organic growth in FY27 (base water revenue: £275m to £308m). If water grows 5 percent instead, revenue is £14m lower. At a 13 to 14 percent drop-through (volume that simply does not arrive), operating profit is £1.9m lower (2.3 percent) and earnings per share about 1.7p lower (75p to 73p). Every water client underspent its first-year allowance, so a water shortfall is the most likely single miss; on its own it is a 2 percent event, not a profit warning.
  2. Rail is flat in FY27 (base: £455m), because reactive volumes near their weather-driven record offset renewals running at 83 percent of plan. If rail falls 3 percent on a mild winter and a Budget-driven deferral of renewals, revenue is £14m lower. At a 20 to 25 percent decremental margin (crews paid for work withdrawn at short notice), operating profit is £2.7m to £3.4m lower (3.3 to 4.1 percent) and earnings per share about 2.5p to 3.1p lower. Rail carries the group's highest margin (7 to 8 percent) and its fixed crews, so a given revenue miss in rail costs almost twice what the same miss costs in water.
  3. Judgements 1 and 2 together form the deferral scenario, and the two are correlated through one macro channel (the finances of the Treasury and of the regulators) and one seasonal channel (a mild winter). In the deferral scenario, group organic growth falls from 4.5 to about 2 percent, and the margin falls from 6.5 to 5.5-6.0 percent (on the company's own calibration, a 10 percent swing in productive volume moves the margin about 170 basis points). Operating profit falls to about £70m to £74m against £82.7m, and earnings per share to 64p to 68p, down 10 to 15 percent. The January 2025 cut was 9 percent of profit; the deferral scenario is the same size on a larger fixed cost base. Cash stays positive and the dividend is held.
  4. Acquisitions continue at £30m to £40m a year. If the deal cadence stops (because prices reach 8 to 10 times EBITDA, private equity competes, or the new chair pauses to review), FY28 earnings per share is about 80p against the model's 82p to 83p (minus 3 percent) and FY29 about 84p against 88p to 89p (minus 5 percent). The model then converges on consensus, and cash builds instead, by about £35m a year. If a £50m buyback replaces a year of deals, earnings per share rises 6 percent, net of about £1.5m of forgone interest income. This judgement is management's to make, and it accounts for the whole of the model's premium to consensus beyond FY27.
  5. The multiple holds between 11.0 and 11.6 times. Each turn of the multiple is worth 8.6 percent of the share price. In the deferral scenario, 9.8 to 10 times on 66p of FY27 earnings gives 650p to 660p (minus 31 to 32 percent); on the dashboard's 24-month-forward basis, with FY28 earnings also cut to about 72p, it gives 700p to 720p (minus 25 percent). The upside branch (organic growth of 6 to 7 percent, a margin of 6.7 to 6.8 percent, earnings per share of 79p to 81p) at 12.5 to 13 times gives 1,000p to 1,050p on FY27 earnings and 1,100p to 1,150p on 24-month-forward earnings (plus 15 to 20 percent). The asymmetry in price is larger than the asymmetry in earnings, because a 10 percent miss costs two turns of multiple while a 5 percent beat earns only one.

A miss is discovered, not announced. The company reports one segment, gives no numeric guidance and discloses contract assets only twice a year. The trading update is the reliable early signal: the January 2025 warning came in one, and the next falls in early April 2027. The order book, defined as firm twelve-month task orders and covering 80 percent of next year's revenue, is a genuine leading indicator, unlike peers' multi-year "secured workload".

Between results, the drivers must be tracked through the clients' documents, not Renew's.

The stock's mechanics amplify any miss. About £1.6m of shares trade a day, 100 percent of analysts rate the shares a Buy, the narrative comes from a single house, and the last forecast cut, of 9 percent, produced a 22 percent one-day fall. A 10 percent earnings miss is therefore a 25 to 35 percent price event, while a 5 percent beat is a 10 to 15 percent one.

The tail (about 5 percent probability): earnings down 25 percent, the multiple at 9 times and the shares below 500p. Four events could cause it: a serious safety incident leading to suspension of accreditation; a material re-cut of Renew's Network Rail position at the Control Period 8 re-let under Great British Railways (bids in 2028-2029, start in April 2029; the largest three-year risk, and the one nobody covering the stock discusses); a Thames Water payment freeze; or a write-down of unbilled contract assets (£5m to £15m).

Renew avoids most of the usual causes of contractor underperformance. United Kingdom contractors have underperformed for four reasons: losses on fixed-price megaprojects (Carillion, Balfour Beatty in 2013-2015, Galliford Try in 2017, Kier in 2019); working-capital unwinds and reverse factoring (Kier); diversification abroad, outside the home regime (Keller's Austral, Balfour Beatty's United States civils); and dips at control-period transitions (Van Elle and Vp at the start of Control Period 7). Renew has none of the first two, one toe in the third (Full Circle) and a demonstrated instance of the fourth (January 2025), from which it recovered within nine months. Contractors have outperformed when they converted a visible regulated cycle into organic growth with stable margins and cash, which is what Renew is doing.

Three dated tests decide the case and form the monitoring plan. The first test's threshold is second-half organic growth of 7 percent, not 8 percent, because the difference is acquired contribution. In the third test, a reversal (acquired growth overtaking organic growth) is the "false friend" path from #5.

Where I differ from the market. The narrative mentions the first-half comparison but does not weight it; it does not treat the house broker's own £30m working-capital outflow as a risk; and it does not discuss Control Period 8 under Great British Railways at all. Earlier Viewforth work also carried a milder deferral branch (a 6.0 percent margin) than the company's own operating-leverage calibration implies (5.5 to 6.0 percent; see #5).

What would change my view. Passing both dated tests would cut the deferral probability from 20 to 25 percent to about 10 percent and move the case from "turning up, unconfirmed" to "reinforcing". A Budget that protects rail and roads capital would do half of that on its own.

Score: 58.A simple, traceable, low-leverage case whose fundamental tail is thin, held back by one undisclosed timing variable that lands inside half-years, an illiquid share register that turns a 10 percent miss into a 30 percent fall, and a client-side risk calendar that is front-loaded into the next six months.

10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The dashboard's rule says Bottoming; my view is "turning up, unconfirmed". The dashboard's phase drives the guideline fair multiple in #11. Renew's operations and its multiple have both turned, but no printed result has yet confirmed the turn.

The operational turn includes the second-half acceleration that management promised in May and delivered by October. The turn in the multiple, back to the ten-year median, recovers the whole of the earlier de-rating and nothing more. The second-half FY26 organic growth rate remains an inference, not a printed figure, until 24 November.

The three inputs the lifecycle question names all point to "turned but not yet proved".

  • Momentum is absent (#8), which argues for Bottoming or Stalling.
  • Scope for upgrades is small and dated (#7), which argues against Reinforcing.
  • Risk factors are front-loaded and negatively skewed over six months, then neutral to positive (#9), which is the signature of a stock that has turned but not yet proved it.

History offers a precedent for each outcome. Renew's own 2019 shows the positive path: a 9 times multiple at a control-period start, then a re-rating to 12 times in December 2019 when the organic growth print confirmed the recovery. Bravida and Instalco in 2024-2025 show the negative path: acquired growth masking organic decay, a de-rating to 10 to 12 times, and a re-rating only when an external upgrade cycle (data centres) arrived.

So what: on these odds, waiting for the 24 November results is cheap. In a turning-up phase, the next two results move the multiple one or two turns in either direction, and the fair multiple is lower than in a Reinforcing phase because the forecasts are less certain. Turning up is also the phase in which the stock is cheapest to own if the turn is real. The cost of waiting for confirmation is the re-rating from 11.6 to 12.5-13 times (plus 8 to 12 percent); the cost of being early is the deferral branch (minus 25 to 35 percent).

Where I differ from the market. The dashboard's mechanical Bottoming reading and the sell-side's implicit Reinforcing reading (three Buys, with targets 27 to 51 percent above the share price) are both wrong, in opposite directions.

What would change my view. Passing the November and May tests would move the phase to Reinforcing; a spring 2027 warning would move it back to Bottoming at a lower price; a chair-led reset with a buyback would move it to Thesis-broadening.

Score: 50.A stock whose fundamentals have turned up and whose market indicators have not yet followed; neither the bottom nor the broadening is on offer, and the next two prints decide which.

11The fair multiple

My fair multiple is 11.0 to 11.6 times, with 11.0 times as the central figure for the 18-month horizon. That range sits above Viewforth's guideline of 10.79 times and below the sell-side's 12.3 to 13 times; its central figure is modestly below today's 11.57 times.

The guideline is mechanical. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for a Bottoming stock is the 30th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history of 24-month-forward price-to-earnings multiples: 10.79 times for Renew, 7 percent below today's 11.57 times. Over five years the multiple has ranged from 8.7 to 15.6 times. The 15.6 times peak in May 2024 reflected the building exit plus a year of 16.6 percent organic growth; the 9.1 times trough in February 2025 reflected the profit warning.

Why start below the median
The guideline's logic about the phase is right: revisions are flat, the technical rating is D, the organic recovery is inferred rather than printed, and the market regime does not pay for visibility alone.
Why not as low as 10.79 times
In the last two years the stock has reached 10.79 times only in the January-to-April 2025 warning window and in three single months since (August and September 2025, March 2026), and each time it recovered to 11 to 12 times within two months. The guideline embeds the deferral branch as if it were the base case.
Why not the median of 11.6 times
A flat-revision stock in a regime that pays for rising revisions should not sit at its median until the organic growth rate is printed, and the 18-month event calendar is negatively skewed.

Three facts place Renew in the "conservative" band rather than the "crash-adjacent" one:

  1. The margin and cash held through a control-period transition: the January 2025 warning cut profit expectations by 9 percent, and operating profit still grew.
  2. 80 percent of next year's revenue sits in a conservatively defined order book.
  3. The multiple is driven by the company and the regime, not the sector: 90 percent of daily share-price variance is idiosyncratic, so the sector's de-rating names (Bilfinger, Spie) do not drag Renew's multiple down.

The fair multiple moves with the phase. If the November and May tests are passed and a reset is announced, the stock enters a delivery phase and the fair multiple becomes the 75th percentile, 12.6 times (the level of autumn 2025 and January 2026). In a deferral, the 10th percentile of 9.8 times is where the shares have historically found buyers within months (April 2025, March 2026).

Peers confirm that Renew sits where a contractor without an upgrade cycle should. Deutsche Bank's target rests on 12.3 times FY27 earnings and a "fair" multiple of 13 times derived from a 27 percent return on capital. Morgan Sindall trades at about 12.9 times, Kier at 10.5 times, Keller at a record 13 times after its upgrade cycle, Balfour Beatty at 13 times 2027 earnings after buybacks, and the continental industrial-services names at 9 to 16.5 times depending on momentum. At 11.0 to 11.6 times, Renew sits where a United Kingdom contractor with a double-digit return on capital, no leverage and no upgrade cycle should: above Kier, and below the names with capital returns and upgrades.

Where I differ from the market. I am below the sell-side (12.3 to 13 times) and above the guideline (10.79 times). The sell-side's multiple requires an upgrade or capital-return narrative that Renew does not have; the guideline's multiple requires a deferral that the base case does not contain.

What would change my view. A buyback or a capital markets day would move my fair multiple to 12.6 times; a spring 2027 warning would move it to 9.8 to 10.5 times on cut earnings; a Budget that cuts rail and roads capital in real terms would move it to 10.8 times without waiting for the results.

Score: 48.The multiple sits at its own median with no re-rating mechanism in sight and a near-term event calendar that argues for the conservative band; the fair multiple is modestly below today's, not far below it.

12Total shareholder return

The 18-month expected return is roughly nil to plus 3 percent: modest, earnings-driven and negatively skewed. Beyond 18 months the skew turns positive, and the three-year return at my fair multiple is a fair 5 to 7 percent a year.

At the guideline multiple of 10.79 times, the model's return is plus 3.5 percent over 18 months and plus 11.1 percent over three years. From 959p, value per share including dividends reaches 992p at the 18-month column (30 September 2027), plus 3.5 percent or plus 3.7 percent annualised, and 1,066p at the three-year column (31 March 2029), plus 11.1 percent or plus 4.4 percent annualised. The chart shows the template's split of each return into dividends, earnings and the multiple.

How to read the template's split. The template's earnings and multiple components both look larger than they are, because the template measures today's multiple on nearer-year earnings (about 13 times the FY26-FY27 blend) and the fair multiple on 24-month-forward earnings. The two exaggerations offset, and the net result is right: the share price is roughly flat over 18 months (plus 21 percent from earnings and minus 17.6 percent from the multiple compound to minus 0.3 percent), so the return is the dividend.

The cleaner view uses the dashboard's own 24-month-forward basis. Today the shares trade at 11.57 times about 83p. At 30 September 2027 the 24-month-forward earnings per share is about 88p to 89p (plus 7 percent); at 10.79 times, that gives about 955p, and about 36p of dividends takes the total to 992p, plus 3.5 percent. At March 2029, 24-month-forward earnings per share of about 93p (plus 12 percent) at 10.79 times gives about 1,006p, and about 60p of dividends takes the total to 1,066p, plus 11.1 percent.

At the guideline multiple, three years of 7 to 9 percent earnings growth buys only a 4 percent annual return, because the de-rating gives back a third of that growth.

At my fair multiple of 11.0 to 11.6 times, the return is about plus 5.5 to 11 percent over 18 months and plus 13 to 19 percent over three years (5 to 7 percent a year). At 11.0 times the share price reaches about 975p in 18 months (plus 1.7 percent before dividends of 3.8 percent) and about 1,025p in three years (plus 7 percent before dividends of 6.2 percent). At 11.6 times it reaches about 1,028p and 1,080p. The return comes from earnings and is modest; the absence of a re-rating mechanism, not the earnings, is what caps it. The dividend (a 2.2 percent yield, growing 5 percent a year) provides a third of the return.

Score: 42.A modest, earnings-driven, negatively skewed 18-month return at the median multiple, improving to a fair 5 to 7 percent a year over three years; most European quality compounders offer more skew for the same visibility.

13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Renew is a genuinely good business of a rare type. It is a listed pure play on legislated, non-discretionary, five-year-funded maintenance of United Kingdom infrastructure, with a scarcity moat (accredited crews and incumbency), a flat 6.5 percent margin that has survived a decade of inflation and a control-period shock, 22 to 27 percent returns on capital, net cash, and a management team that under-promises and delivers within 2 percent in ordinary years. Its growth has turned from a shallow trough, and the three growth pools it sells into (water, grid and roads) are all in ramp phases to FY29.

The investment case, however, is thin on the 18-month view. The market already holds our base case (FY27 earnings per share of about 76p, a 6.5 percent margin) with no cushion, at the median multiple, in a regime that pays for rising revisions and self-funded returns, neither of which Renew offers. The one variable that moves the number, when regulated clients call off work, cannot be seen until it has happened, and it is skewed to the downside through spring 2027 (the Budget, Great British Railways, the first-half rail comparison and water-client finances). The stock's mechanics then turn a 10 percent earnings miss into a 30 percent fall. Renew's cash record is sound but is not the serial beat the narrative claims, and the working-capital path is the open question for 24 November.

Renew's edge over the market lies beyond 18 months, and it is a thin edge. The skew then turns positive: an acquisition drip that consensus excludes, a water and grid peak in 2027-2029, and a new chair with a record of resetting targets and returning cash. The edge is that pair of unpriced options, net of an unpriced Control Period 8 risk.

What I would do: not buy today, and set two buy triggers. The 18-month expected return at my fair multiple, weighted by probability, is roughly nil to plus 3 percent.

  1. Trigger 1: a deferral-driven sell-off to 9.8 to 10.5 times. The order book, the net cash and the recovery of operating leverage make that sell-off a buyable event, as 2025 showed.
  2. Trigger 2: the 24 November and May 2027 results pass the tests in #9, together with a dated capital markets day. The multiple can then revisit 12.5 to 13 times, and the case becomes a Reinforcing compounder worth owning for the FY28-FY29 peak.

Between results, monitor the water clients' and Network Rail's documents, not Renew's.

The four headline ratings

C
Thesis's Change Forces' Strength
Legislated demand to 2030 and a completed power platform are real forces, but they transmit into Renew's earnings at 6 to 8 percent a year on a flat margin with no acceleration in sight; the only force that could lift the growth rate (the chair) has announced nothing.
B
Foundations' Robustness
A 22 to 27 percent return on capital, net cash, a margin range held for a decade through inflation and a control-period shock, 95 percent framework retention and a two-decade delivery record put the foundations in the top quarter of listed European companies. They fall short of an A because there is no pricing power, Network Rail is 40 percent of revenue, and the chief financial officer carries three jobs.
C
Setups' Fit/Crispness
The case is a hybrid of two setups and fits neither cleanly. It is partly a cause for concern (the Control Period 7 deferral) that has mostly cleared in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business whose multiple has already reverted to its median, so it does not fit "CfC Clearing on a Q1/Q2 multiple" (the low multiple is no longer there). It is partly a serial acquirer whose mechanical upgrades are 1 to 2 percent a year, so it does not fit "Delivering - Serial Acquirer - Mechanical EPS Upgrader" either (the upgrades are too small, and the sell-side momentum rating is D).
C
Case Riskiness
The case is simple in structure and low-risk in fundamentals, but one undisclosed timing variable lands inside half-years, the next six months carry a front-loaded client-side risk calendar with a 20 to 25 percent probability of deferral, and an illiquid register with a single-house narrative makes the share-price reaction to any miss three times the earnings effect.

  1. Authorship and date. Written 22 October 2026 by the Investment Analyst for Richard.
  2. Market data. Share price 959p on 16 October 2026; market value about £760m on 79.2m shares; about £1.6m of shares traded a day.
  3. Reporting calendar. Renew's fiscal year ends 30 September. FY26 (the year to 30 September 2026) has closed and was reported "in line, net cash ahead" on 1 October 2026; the FY26 results are due on 24 November 2026. The last reported period is the half-year to 31 March 2026.
  4. Units. Money is in pounds sterling and per-share figures are in pence, unless a chart states otherwise. Revenue growth is on the company's basis (including its share of joint ventures) unless stated.
  5. "Consensus" is the FactSet median of three brokers: Deutsche Bank (which is also Renew's house broker and nominated adviser), Peel Hunt and Shore Capital.
  6. "The model" is the Financial Analyst's model after update 2; this memo uses its forecasts.
  7. Statutory against company revenue growth. The model's FY26 revenue growth prints as +10.4 percent on FactSet's statutory base (£1,081m, which excludes the £35m joint-venture share); on the company's basis it is +6.9 percent.
  8. Cash outside adjusted profit. The "acquisitions and legacy cash" line in the forecast table includes £3m to £7m a year of cash that adjusted profit excludes: employment-linked deferred consideration, Allenbuild legacy claims and exceptional deal costs.
  9. Working-capital change made by this memo. This memo has moved the model's working-capital input toward the house broker's assumption (see inputs-changed.md). The effect is cash-only: about £5m lower net cash in each year, with no material effect on earnings per share.
  10. Visual sources. Charts not otherwise sourced are drawn from the figures in this memo.
